501: Memory. What if you never forgot anything?
502: Every name. Every birthday. Every page of every book you've ever read.
503: For a small group of people, part of that is real. It's called highly superior autobiographical memory.
504: Pick a random date from fifteen years ago, and they can often tell you what day of the week it was, and what they did.
505: Scientists have confirmed only a few dozen cases. And many of them call it a mixed gift. The bad days don't fade either.
506: Nearly a century ago, a Russian journalist named Solomon Shereshevsky could repeat long lists of numbers, even years later.
507: But he had the opposite problem. He couldn't easily forget. Ordinary conversations were hard to follow, because every word set off a flood of images.
508: So let's run a test. Memory dial at maximum. A surprise quiz: forty random facts, read once.
509: You ace it. Forty out of forty.
510: The next morning, you also remember every advert on the way there. Every number plate. Every awkward thing you have ever said.
511: And here's the strange part. Your memory isn't a video recording. Every time you remember something, your brain rebuilds it.
512: In a famous experiment from nineteen seventy-four, people watched a film of a car crash. Then they were asked how fast the cars were going when they smashed into each other. Or when they hit each other.
513: One word changed the memory. The smashed group guessed higher speeds. A week later, about a third of them remembered broken glass. There was none.
514: Quick side note: that's why scientists call memory reconstructive. It's less like a hard drive, and more like retelling a story.
515: And forgetting isn't a bug either. Researchers think it helps your brain drop the clutter, and keep the patterns that actually matter.
516: A perfect memory would be a perfect archive, and a terrible filter.
517: Verdict: forgetting is housekeeping. Let's set memory back to normal, and try the dial everyone wants. Speed.
